Section 01

A Case Study

01

The scenario: a former industrial site, before redevelopment

A consulting firm is hired to assess lead contamination on a 2-hectare former battery-manufacturing site before it is redeveloped into a residential park. For this hypothetical case, the decision rule requires the one-sided 95% upper confidence limit for the site-wide mean soil lead concentration to be below 400 mg/kg.
Keep the four lectures in mind as we walk through what this firm actually did, and where it went wrong.

The decision this report needed to support

In this hypothetical case, redevelopment could proceed only if the one-sided 95% upper confidence limit for the site-wide mean soil lead concentration was below 400 mg/kg. That sentence captures the decision-rule core of the simplified DQO workflow from Lecture 3: a decision, a confidence level, and an explicit threshold.
Every choice the firm made, sample mass, sample count, statistics, should trace back to satisfying exactly this requirement, and nothing more. Keep this sentence in mind as we look at what they actually did.

What went wrong: the report was rejected

All 20 cores were taken at a fixed 30 cm depth. A regulator's own confirmation samples, taken at multiple depths, found a buried dumping layer at 80 cm with lead concentrations over 3 times higher.
{{ revealFail.prompt }}
This is a design and representativeness failure, not a statistics failure. The interval may have been calculated correctly for the sampled 30 cm domain, but it did not apply to the intended site-wide soil population because the design never gave the buried layer a chance to be captured. No amount of statistical rigor fixes a plan that samples the wrong location.
Section 02

Common Pitfalls in Practice

02

The math was right. The plan was wrong.

If you handed a statistician just the firm's twenty data points, they could compute a mathematically valid interval for the sampled 30 cm domain, and it might sit comfortably below 400 mg/kg. The failure is not arithmetic; it is a mismatch between the sampled domain and the target population.
The failure is entirely upstream of the statistics: in the sampling design itself, which never gave the buried contamination layer any chance of being included in those twenty data points. This is why representativeness and design errors are so dangerous, they can hide perfectly behind flawless-looking math.

Five mistakes that keep recurring in practice

{{ p.label }}
{{ p.desc }}

Convenience bias: sampling where it's easy, not where it matters

Field crews under time or budget pressure gravitate toward accessible locations - near a road, at a shallow depth, away from obstacles - rather than the locations a randomized or systematic design actually specifies.
{{ revealConv.prompt }}
This is exactly the failure mode in the case study: the fixed 30 cm depth was easy and consistent to execute, but it was not chosen because the design called for it - it was chosen because it was convenient, and it missed the buried layer entirely.

Undersized n: skipping the calculation and guessing

A distinct pitfall from convenience bias: here, the locations might be perfectly reasonable, but the number of samples was chosen by budget or habit ("we always take ten"), rather than calculated from the sample-size equation in Lecture 2 against a real target margin of error.
The result is a confidence interval far wider than the decision can tolerate, or in the worst case, a plan that never even checks. Every sampling plan should show its n calculation, not just its final sample count, so this exact pitfall is auditable.

Pitfall, consequence, and fix

PitfallConsequenceFix Convenience samplingMisses locations the design intended to coverFollow the randomized/systematic plan exactly, even when inconvenient Undersized nCI too wide to support the required decisionUse the sample-size equation before going to the field, not after Ignoring particle sizeSample mass too small for coarse, heterogeneous materialApply Gy's theory; increase mass with the cube of particle diameter Compositing when a hot spot mattersAverages away the exact signal you needed to detectKeep discrete samples whenever a maximum or location matters, not just a mean Broken chain of custodyEvidentiary value is weakened and the data may be rejectedDocument every transfer, every time, without exception
Section 03

Synthesis: The Whole Unit

03

Over-compositing: averaging away exactly the signal you needed

Compositing reduces variance, which sounds good, but it also destroys the ability to see any single sub-sample's value. If the regulatory question is "is there a hot spot," rather than "what is the average," an over-composited sample can hide the exact result the investigation needed.
This connects directly back to Lecture 2: compositing k sub-samples divides variance roughly by k, but it also means you only ever see one averaged number. Choosing to composite is choosing to trade away location-specific information, a decision that should be made deliberately, not by default.

Broken chain of custody: perfect data, inadmissible result

A missing signature, an unexplained storage-temperature gap, or mismatched sample IDs can undermine an otherwise flawless analytical result, not because the chemistry is wrong, but because no one can prove the sample that was analyzed is the sample that was actually collected.
In a regulatory or legal proceeding, a custody gap can weaken evidentiary value and may cause data to be qualified or rejected. Of the five pitfalls, this is the one purely about paperwork discipline, and the one with zero excuse for occurring.

Integrative example: redesign the case-study plan so it would pass regulatory review.

Section 04

Check Your Understanding

04

Ignoring particle size: applying the wrong Gy's-theory mass

A sample mass calculated for a fine, homogeneous powder is dramatically too small for a coarse, gravelly material, remember, required mass scales with particle diameter cubed. Using a "standard" sample mass regardless of material coarseness is a direct violation of Gy's theory from Lecture 1.
This pitfall is easy to prevent: always check the maximum particle size of the actual material before finalizing sample mass, never assume last project's mass calculation carries over to a new site.

Unit Takeaways

The sample is the foundation; everything else is downstream

  • Sampling error can exceed instrumental error by a wide margin, especially for heterogeneous targets.
  • Gy's theory and the sample-size equation let you size a plan to a stated, defensible precision before you go to the field.
  • QA/QC samples and chain of custody make a result both scientifically and legally defensible.
  • Most real-world failures are design and representativeness failures - not statistics failures.
